items.prompt: What does legibility mean for a design?
choices: A newcomer can read it and predict what it does
It uses the fewest lines of code it can
Its author can explain it from memory
items.explanation: Legibility is about the reader with no context, not about length or the author's own fluency.

items.prompt: A design is compact but only its author can read it. It is best called...
choices: Legible, because short code is always easy for anyone to read
Robust, because fewer lines always means fewer hidden bugs in it
Clever, because it leans on the author's insight
items.explanation: Compact is not the same as readable by others. Reliance on the author's insight is what makes it clever.

items.prompt: Who should a long-lived design be written for?
choices: The author, who knows it best
The reader who arrives later with no context
The compiler and the build tooling it must pass through
items.explanation: The author leaves; the design stays. The later reader is the one who has to live with it.

items.prompt: Why is Renata's mini-language risky here?
choices: Mini-languages are never a valid pattern
Only she can read it, and she is leaving
It cannot express any real entitlement rule
items.explanation: The pattern itself is legitimate. The risk comes from who inherits it and when the author becomes unavailable.

items.prompt: A typo in a custom-language rule string is usually caught...
choices: At run time, by a hand-written parser
Before shipping, by the compiler's checks
By the editor, as the author types it
items.explanation: Strings in a home-made language get no help from the compiler or editor, so mistakes tend to surface late.

items.prompt: What does the plain version of the design cost?
choices: A grammar every reader must first learn
Errors that only appear when it runs
More lines of code for each rule
items.explanation: More text is the plain version's price. The other two costs belong to the mini-language.

items.prompt: Two designs cost the same to build. One is clever, one legible. Which does this unit favour?
choices: The clever one, because it shows more skill
Whichever one the original author finds more elegant and quick
The legible one, for the reader with no context
items.explanation: With equal cost, the tie-breaker is who will change the design later, and that reader has no context.

items.prompt: What is the bill that cleverness leaves for later?
choices: Fees for the tools the author happened to use
Time newcomers spend decoding what the author meant
Extra memory consumed on the production servers
items.explanation: The cost is human: each future change starts with decoding the design.

items.prompt: Two designs do the same job. One stores rules in a compact custom language only its author is fluent in. The other uses named functions and is about three times longer. The author leaves in six months and rules change rarely. Which is the better long-term choice?
choices: The named functions, because later changers will not share the author's context
The compact language, because shorter text always means fewer defects later
The compact language, because the author can document the grammar after leaving
The named functions, because custom languages are never acceptable in a codebase
items.explanation: Rare changes and a departing author make reader context the deciding factor. The reasoning is about who changes it, not a ban on custom languages.
items.reference:
Who changes the design later?
clever: compact, relies on the author's insight
legible: a newcomer can predict what it does
the later reader has no context and no one to ask
similar cost: choose the legible one
Why: a long-lived design is judged by the reader who arrives after the author leaves.
items.learnMore:
Legibility versus cleverness

Cleverness buys compactness for someone who already understands the design; legibility buys safe change for someone who does not. Over a long life, the second kind of reader does most of the changing.

Common mistake

Treating a clever design as wrong in itself. It is a cost to weigh against who will maintain it, not a rule.
items.reflection: Think of a system you use that only one person truly understands. What would it take for a stranger to take it over safely?

items.prompt: Which is the strongest evidence that a design is legible?
choices: The author can explain every rule in under one minute without notes
It has the fewest lines of any alternative that was considered
A teammate who never saw it correctly predicts what a rule does from reading it
Every test passes after the author's most recent change to it
items.explanation: Legibility is tested on a newcomer. Author fluency, brevity and passing tests all hold for clever designs too.

items.prompt: The clever design can express rules the plain design cannot, yet no requested rule needs that. What is the right reading?
choices: The extra power is free, so having it just in case is worthwhile
The extra power is unneeded today, while the legibility cost is real
The plain design is under-built and must be replaced at once and rewritten
The clever design is wrong in principle for any team to adopt
items.explanation: Unused capability still has to be understood by every future reader. Weigh it against actual requirements, not possibilities.

items.prompt: When does preferring the legible design stop being the right call?
choices: When the author plans to stay on the team for several more years
When the clever version is shorter than the plain one by a third
When the clever version comes with more tests than the plain one
When the real problem genuinely needs that complexity
items.explanation: Legibility means matching complexity to the real problem. A simple design that does not fit the need is under-built, not legible.

items.prompt: What is a one-way door?
choices: A decision costly to reverse once others depend on it
A decision only one person is allowed to make
A decision that is made once and never reviewed
items.explanation: The door image is about reversal cost, not about who decides or how often it is reviewed.

items.prompt: What is a two-way door?
choices: A decision that is cheap to undo if it proves wrong
A decision that two teams must approve together
A decision that offers exactly two possible options to choose from
items.explanation: A two-way door can be walked back through cheaply, so it needs little ceremony.

items.prompt: Swapping the inside of a private function nothing else calls is...
choices: A one-way door
Impossible to classify
A two-way door
items.explanation: Nothing outside depends on it, so undoing it affects only you.

items.prompt: Which decision earns a second reviewer first?
choices: A local variable name inside one small private function
A stored format other services will write to
A comment placed above a private helper function in one file
items.explanation: A format others write to is hard to take back, so it deserves the most scrutiny.

items.prompt: What makes a door one-way?
choices: The code behind it is very long
Other work comes to depend on it
It was decided in a long meeting
items.explanation: Dependents, not size or process, turn a decision into a commitment.

items.prompt: A public config syntax other services write to is likely...
choices: A one-way door
A two-way door
Not a design decision at all
items.explanation: Once rules are written in the syntax, changing it means migrating all of them.

items.prompt: How should caution relate to reversibility?
choices: More caution the faster a change ships
The same caution for every single decision the team makes
More caution the harder a decision is to undo
items.explanation: Caution is a limited budget; spend it where mistakes are expensive to fix.

items.prompt: A quick chat message is enough process for which decision?
choices: A format that many services will store in their databases
A public interface that other teams already call from code
A change that is cheap to undo inside one module
items.explanation: Cheap-to-reverse changes need little process; the other two are commitments.

items.prompt: A rule engine looks like an internal detail. Three weeks later, two services store their rules as strings in its syntax. What has happened to the door?
choices: It stayed two-way, because one team still owns the engine's code
It was always one-way, since interpreters cannot ever be removed once they are in use
It became one-way, because the syntax is now a format others depend on
Nothing changed, because doors are set by the author's intent
items.explanation: The engine's code did not change, but its syntax became a contract once others stored data in it.
items.reference:
Spend caution by reversibility
two-way door: cheap to undo, decide and adjust
one-way door: others build on it, slow down
test: what does undoing it cost once others depend on it?
watch for stored formats and public syntax
Why: the cost of reversal, not the size of the code, sets how much scrutiny a decision deserves.
items.learnMore:
One-way and two-way doors

A decision is a one-way door when undoing it means changing other people's work, as with a stored format, a syntax others write in, or a public interface. A two-way door can be undone inside your own module.

Common mistake

Calling something reversible because its owner could delete the code. What matters is what has come to depend on it.
items.reflection: Pick a choice in your own life, such as a lease or a tool you taught your whole team. Is it a one-way or two-way door, and how do you know?

items.prompt: Which question best separates a one-way door from a two-way door?
choices: How many lines were changed when the code was first written down?
How confident was the author on the day the decision was made?
What would undoing this cost once others have built on it?
Which programming language was the decision implemented in by the team?
items.explanation: Reversal cost in the presence of dependents is the whole distinction. The other questions do not predict it.

items.prompt: Which choice most deserves a second reviewer and a written record?
choices: Renaming a local variable for clarity inside one module
The layout of a stored file format other services write to
Reordering two private helper functions within one file
Changing the indentation style across every file in a single repository
items.explanation: Only the stored format has external dependents, which is what makes it hard to reverse.

choices: Correct, since the team owns the interpreter
Correct, as long as the deletion lands in a single pull request

Deleting it breaks every rule already stored in its syntax
items.explanation: The question is not whether the owner can delete code but what happens to what depends on it.

items.prompt: What does an ADR record?
choices: Every line of code changed that week
What was decided, why, and what was rejected
Who attended each planning meeting
items.explanation: An ADR keeps reasoning, which code and meeting lists do not.

items.prompt: Where should an ADR live?
choices: Checked in next to the code
Only in a chat thread
In a slide deck shared once with the team
items.explanation: Next to the code it can be found and versioned; chat and memory fade.

items.prompt: Which ADR part answers 'why did we not do the obvious clever thing?'
choices: Rejected alternatives
The status line at the top
The title of the document itself
items.explanation: That section lists the clever option and the reasons it was turned down.

items.prompt: Code shows what was built. What does it not show?
choices: Which functions currently exist
What the variables are called
Why one working option beat another
items.explanation: Reasons for a choice are not visible in the result of that choice.

items.prompt: Why can a chat thread not replace an ADR?
choices: It is always too short to be useful
It disappears long before the code does
It cannot hold any text longer than a single sentence
items.explanation: Chats get archived, searched poorly or lost; the code outlives them.

items.prompt: The four ADR parts, in order, are...
choices: Decision, status, author, date of approval
Context, decision, rejected alternatives, consequences
Rejected, context, tests, deployment plan
items.explanation: The order walks from the problem to what the choice leaves behind.

items.prompt: What is the 'Consequences' section for?
choices: What the decision makes easier, harder or riskier
A list of the people who should answer for it if it fails
Test results from the most recent build on the main branch
items.explanation: It tells the next reader what they have inherited with the choice.

items.prompt: An ADR is written mainly for...
choices: Management, to approve the work beforehand
The compiler, so it can check every type involved in it
Someone who will ask why after the author is gone
items.explanation: The audience is the future reader with a question and no one to ask.

items.prompt: A new engineer proposes the mini-language Renata already rejected. Which single ADR section most directly pre-empts that proposal?
choices: Rejected alternatives, with the reason each was turned down
Context, describing the team size, the product and the constraints
Status, showing the record was formally accepted
Decision, naming the design that was chosen
items.explanation: Only the rejected-alternatives section addresses the specific idea being proposed and why it lost.
items.reference:
Four parts of a decision record
context: the problem and constraints
decision: what was chosen
rejected alternatives: what else, and why not
consequences: what gets easier, harder, riskier
Why: the code shows what was built, but only the record keeps why a working alternative was turned down.
items.learnMore:
Architecture decision records

An ADR is short, kept next to the code, and written for someone who will ask a question after the author is gone. The rejected-alternatives section pre-empts the exact proposal a newcomer is most likely to bring.

Common mistake

Writing the record as approval paperwork before the fact and leaving out what was rejected. The rejected options are the part nobody can reconstruct later.
items.reflection: Think of a decision you made that others later questioned. What would a short written record of the alternatives have saved you from explaining?

items.prompt: Which of these ADRs would help a stranger most?
choices: One describing the chosen design in great detail along with its full test plan
One listing everyone consulted and the date of every meeting that was held
One naming the choice, rejected options with reasons, and costs
One copying the final code with a comment written on every single line
items.explanation: Reasoning and trade-offs are what code and meeting lists cannot reconstruct.

items.prompt: The rules list cannot handle same-day exceptions, and the ADR's consequences say an overrides table does. Why include that line?
choices: It lets the author claim credit for making a second decision
It marks the boundary, so readers neither force the need into this design nor reopen the debate
It proves the overrides table already exists in production
It removes the need for any separate record about the table
items.explanation: Saying what the decision does not cover prevents both a bad fit and a repeated argument.

items.prompt: An ADR exists, but nothing links to it and the system has moved on. What is the best fix?
choices: Delete it, since a stale record misleads more than silence does
Leave it alone, since its age shows the decision was right
Rewrite the old record in place so the history reads cleanly
Link it from the module and say a new record supersedes it
items.explanation: A record is only useful if found, and replacing it explicitly keeps the trail of reasoning intact.

items.prompt: When is reversing the mini-language cheapest?
choices: After a year, once everyone knows it
At any time, since the cost is always exactly the same
On day one, before anything depends on it
items.explanation: With no dependents, only the base removal cost remains.

items.prompt: What makes the reversal cost climb?
choices: More comments being added to the code
More things coming to depend on it
The server hardware getting faster
items.explanation: Each dependent brings a migration cost with it.

items.prompt: With a base of 4 days and 3 days per dependent, what does 0 dependents cost to reverse?
choices: 4 days
3 days
0 days

items.prompt: With a base of 4 days and 3 days per dependent, what do 2 dependents cost?
choices: 10 days
6 days
14 days

items.prompt: With a base of 4 days and 3 days per dependent, what does 1 dependent cost?
choices: 4 days
12 days
7 days

items.prompt: Building the plain version costs 6 days. With 2 dependents, reversing costs 10. Which is greater?
choices: Building the plain version
Reversing the mini-language
Neither; they are exactly equal in cost
items.explanation: 10 days is more than 6 days, so the clever design is now the costlier path.

items.prompt: As lock-in grows, does the decision itself change?
choices: Yes, its code gets rewritten
No, the things around it change
Yes, it turns into another design
items.explanation: The mini-language is the same; what depends on it has grown.

items.prompt: Why is it best to decide before shipping?
choices: Reversal is cheapest while nothing depends on it
Shipping the code makes it run noticeably faster in production
Reviewers are only available before the code ships to users
items.explanation: The cheapest moment to avoid a one-way door is before the first dependent exists.

items.prompt: Reversal costs a base of 4 days plus 3 days per dependent. How much does it cost to reverse with 5 dependents?
choices: 15 days
23 days
19 days
12 days
items.explanation: 4 + 3 x 5 = 19. Forgetting the base gives 15.
items.reference:
Reversal cost = 4 + 3 x dependents (assumed days)
0 dependents: 4 days
2 dependents: 10 days
8 dependents: 28 days
plain version built on day one: 6 days
Why: the decision does not change, but each new dependent adds to what it costs to undo it.
items.learnMore:
Lock-in grows after shipping

On day one the cost to reverse is just the base cost. Every service that stores rules in the syntax adds migration work, so the cost climbs with time even though nothing about the decision changed. The leverage is earliest.

Common mistake

Believing a cost has not been paid so it does not exist. It has been incurred with each dependent, even if nobody has felt it yet.
items.reflection: Pick something in your work that started as a quick experiment. Count what now depends on it; what would it cost to undo today?

items.prompt: The base is 4 days, each dependent adds 3 days, and the plain version costs 6 days. What is the smallest number of dependents at which reversing costs more than 6 days?
choices: 1 dependent, since 4 + 3 = 7 exceeds 6
2 dependents, since 4 + 6 = 10 exceeds 6
3 dependents, since 3 x 3 = 9 exceeds 6
0 dependents, since 4 is close to 6
items.explanation: 0 dependents gives 4, which is under 6. One dependent gives 7, the first value above 6.

items.prompt: Can 'prefer legible' be over-applied?
choices: No, simpler is always better whatever the problem
Only in work that sits outside engineering altogether
Yes, if it rejects a needed abstraction
items.explanation: Rejecting a genuinely needed abstraction can produce something worse.

items.prompt: A giant if/else block nobody can hold in their head is...
choices: The most legible design possible
A clever design, since it hides logic in branches
Not legible, even though it is simple
items.explanation: Legibility is about being understandable, not about looking plain.

items.prompt: Data written by others in your format counts as...
choices: Not a dependent, as no code calls it
A dependent, even if no code calls your module
Owned only by the original author
items.explanation: Stored data in your syntax is a dependent in the same way a caller is.

items.prompt: Designing flexibility for an imagined inheritor risks...
choices: Everyone paying its complexity for nothing, forever
The code running far too quickly
The decision record becoming far too long for anyone to read
items.explanation: Unused flexibility still has to be understood by every reader.

items.prompt: When should you build the general version?
choices: When a second concrete case actually appears
Before any concrete case exists
Whenever the team has some spare time before a release
items.explanation: A real second case shows what the general shape needs to be.

items.prompt: An ADR nobody links to or reads is a failure of...
choices: Compilation speed
Type annotations
Discoverability
items.explanation: The record exists but nobody finds it when the question comes up.

items.prompt: How should an old ADR be retired?
choices: By quietly ignoring it from now on without telling anyone
By writing a new one that says it supersedes the old
By deleting the file and hoping nobody needs it again
items.explanation: An explicit superseding record keeps the trail of reasoning.

items.prompt: The worked example in L3 is...
choices: The complete rule for every design
One case of the judgment, not the whole territory
Proof that the clever option is always wrong in practice
items.explanation: Different audiences and different news would change the answer.

The plain list is proven wrong for every team size
Nothing changes, since the record was already accepted
items.explanation: A changed context can justify revisiting a decision, but through a new, explicit record rather than drift.

Why: legibility means matching complexity to the real problem, not minimising it.
items.learnMore:
Limits of the judgment

Preferring legible designs can fail by under-building, and writing for an imagined inheritor can add complexity nobody needs. The guard against both is a second concrete case: generalise when it appears, not before.

Common mistake

Reading the worked example as a rule that the plain option always wins. It is one case, not the whole territory.
items.reflection: Think of a time you built something flexible for a future need that never came. What signal could have told you to wait?

items.prompt: The mini-language has run for eight months with eight dependents and has no decision record. What does the record's job become?
choices: Choosing the design from scratch as if nothing existed yet and nobody relied on it
Documenting what reversing would cost, so the choice is deliberate
Hiding the history so new owners are not discouraged
Proving that the original author was right all along
items.explanation: Once the door has been walked through, the useful record explains the real costs and options.

A mini-language must be built by one author working alone
A config-time mechanism may be justified by an open-ended need
The record is unnecessary once there are many rule authors

items.prompt: A team builds a plugin system 'for whoever inherits this', yet no second use case exists. Which failure mode is this?
choices: A one-way door disguised as a two-way door
A decision record that nobody ever reads
Over-applying legibility to reject a needed abstraction
Speculative flexibility: everyone pays its complexity for a reader who never needs it
items.explanation: The flexibility is for an imagined reader. The other modes involve dependents, discoverability or under-building.
